newsitem.title: USA: FEATURE-Alaska salmon industry turns to alternative products.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-Alaska salmon industry turns to alternative products.

text.p: The buffet spread at a stylish Anchorage brewpub features many of the usual snacks such as burgers, Teriyaki strips, corn dogs, sausages, pocket sandwiches and fajitas.

But these treats are not the typical restaurant fare. All are made of Alaska salmon, a product in abundant supply -- oversupply, some would say. Tailored for American palates and preferences for convenience and wholesomeness, the products were unveiled recently at the annual "Symphony of Salmon" contest sponsored by the Alaska Seafood Marketing Institute and the Alaska Fisheries Development Foundation.

They may represent salvation for the beleagured Alaska salmon industry, which must make gains with fish-phobic American consumers if it is to avert a crisis, officials said. "I think that's what people want, and that's what they're going to have to get. Otherwise, we're not going to make any inroads in this very difficult time," Donna Parker, a fisheries specialist for the Alaska Department of Commerce, said of the alternative foods.

Tough times for Alaska fishermen result from bumper state salmon harvests that have flooded world markets and halved prices in the past decade. While natural salmon runs elsewhere are depeleted or wiped out, Alaska's streams are jammed, producing record or near-record harvests. Last summer, fishermen dumped some of their harvested salmon at sea rather than leaving it to rot, unsold, in harbours and bays.

Meanwhile, production from salmon farms in Chile, Norway and elsewhere has exploded over the past decade, significantly eroding Alaska's share of the world market. Farmed salmon has started to displace Alaskan salmon even in Japan, traditionally the state's top market. In 1987, Alaska held an 85 percent share of the Japanese salmon market; in 1995, that was down to 53 percent, according to state figures.

Doug Van Devanter, director of sales for Trident Seafoods Corp., said new products appealing to the U.S. market offered the best hope for Alaska salmon fishermen. "We see it as a tremendous opportunity because it's one fish where the world supply is large and growing. The more we can do to develop new products and get Americans to eat more salmon the more it will help us," he said.

The goal is to change perceptions that "salmon is an expensive item that can be served only a few times a year," he said. Ultimately, the battle is against chicken, beef and other meats, not against the growing production of farmed salmon.

"We are really competing with other protein sources more than we are with other salmon sources," said Van Devanter, whose company has been experimenting with new products and trying to sell salmon to chain restaurants, among other buyers.

The cheapest and most plentiful of Alaska's five salmon species is pink salmon, traditionally plopped in cans and eschewed by state residents as low-grade. The major impediment to sales of low-fat pinks, one seller determined, is the clunky can.

North Pacific Seafoods Inc. won a prize in this year's contest for its pink salmon packaged in a convenient foil pouch. The flaky, pre-cooked salmon is meant to compete with tuna for such uses as sandwiches and salads; the pouch offers unlimited shelf life, easy transport and elimation of many trash headaches.

A Tlingit Indian company learned recently, to its officers' surprise, that ethnicity should be emphasised, not downplayed, in packaging. Kake Tribal Corp. changed its salmon-ham and salmon-spread packages to include traditional Tlingit designs from the southeast Alaska rain forest after focus-group tests showed homemakers in the Lower 48 states were attracted to the idea of supporting a Native American business.

Other salmon innovations have come from family stovetops. One past Symphony of Salmon winner grew out of an old family recipe Duff Mitchell enjoyed as a child growing up in Juneau, when he carried dried salmon in his knapsack during hikes up local mountain trails. Now he and his wife are selling a condiment called "Alaskabits," a healthful, smoked-salmon alternative to bacon bits.

This year's Symphony of Salmon grand prize winner was a smoked salmon chowder made by Anchorage-based Trapper's Creek Smoking Co. It and other winners will be displayed at upcoming food trade shows in Boston and Japan.

Sometimes, the secret to marketing success in the U.S. market is to camouflage the salmon taste, apparently. Even the fish's most enthusiastic fans concede the strong flavor of wild Alaska salmon, while prized by gourmands, is viewed with suspicion by many average consumers.

That is why the new products will be important for the U.S. market, said Anne Willan, a chef, author and cooking-school founder who helped judge this year's Symphony of Salmon contestants. "I think that there is a limit to the amount of fresh salmon that people are prepared to eat," she said.
